In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful

Surah Ta-Ha

It is Meccan. It has been said that it is Meccan except for His saying, ﴿Bear patiently what they say﴾ [Ta-Ha: 130] and what follows it, and His saying, ﴿Do not strain your eyes﴾ [Ta-Ha: 131] and what follows it. Its verses number one hundred and thirty-five.

[p-4169]

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful

Discussion of the interpretation of His saying, the Exalted:

[1] ﴿Ta-Ha﴾ [2] ﴿We did not send down the Qur'an to you to make you suffer﴾ [Ta-Ha: 2] [3] ﴿but as a reminder to whoever fears﴾ [Ta-Ha: 3].

﴿Ta-Ha﴾: We have previously stated that the correct view regarding these letters with which the surahs open is that they are names of those surahs. This implies that the surah is composed of them. Nevertheless, their inability to imitate them is the most eloquent sign of its truthfulness. The Imam Ibn al-Qayyim (may God have mercy on him) drew attention to another subtle point in (al-Kafiya al-Shafiya) with his saying:

Consider the surahs that open with its letters; you will find a secret of great importance.

He never brought a surah without a report about the Qur'an following it,

since it is a report about it concerning them. In this is healing for the seeker of faith.

It indicates that its speech is itself and not other than it, and the truth is one of clear exposition.

So consider the beginning of the Book, then after it al-A'raf, then likewise Luqman,

together with what follows it, and also Ha-Mim with Ya-Sin, and understand the requirement of al-Furqan.

﴿We did not send down the Qur'an to you to make you suffer﴾ [Ta-Ha: 2]: that is, so that you would exhaust yourself through excessive grief over them and over their disbelief, and through your distress that they should not believe. The word (al-shaqa') means fatigue. From it comes the proverb: "More wretched than the breaker of a colt."

His saying, the Exalted, ﴿but as a reminder to whoever fears﴾ [Ta-Ha: 3]: that is, a reminder to him. That is: We did not send down the Qur'an to you so that you would wear yourself out by conveying it, but as a reminder for whoever has in his heart fear and tenderness, and is affected by warning. The purpose is that nothing is required of you except to convey and remind, and it has not been decreed upon you that they必 must believe necessarily. The divine practice (al-sunnah al-ilahiyyah) has been followed [p-4170] in addressing the Messenger in several places of the revelation, forbidding him from grieving over them and from being distressed on their account, as in His saying: ﴿So let there be no discomfort in your breast﴾ [al-A'raf: 2], ﴿Perhaps you would destroy yourself with grief over their footsteps﴾ [al-Kahf: 6], and ﴿Do not let those who race to disbelief grieve you﴾. This verse is also of this kind.

In all of this there is an honouring of the Messenger, may the blessings of God be upon him, and a fine care and tenderness for him, which is not hidden. Then he pointed to the magnification of the status of this noble revelation, by attributing it to the One who is singular in His attributes and His acts, with his saying:

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 20, verses 4–5:

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, Exalted is He:

[4] ﴿A revelation from He who created the earth and the high heavens.﴾ [5] ﴿The Most Merciful is established upon the Throne.﴾ [Ta-Ha: 5].

﴿A revelation from He who created the earth and the high heavens﴾ ﴿The Most Merciful﴾ [Ta-Ha: 5] is read in the nominative (raf') as a praise (madh), meaning: He is the Most Merciful. It is also read in the genitive (jarr), as an attribute (sifah) of the relative pronoun (mawsul). As for His saying, ﴿is established upon the Throne﴾, it means: He rose above and ascended. This was said by Ibn Jarir. Later scholars (al-Khalaf) have gone to make this a metaphor (majaz) for dominion and sovereignty, as in their saying: "So-and-so sat upon the throne of kingship," even if he did not actually sit on the throne at all.

The discussion of this has already preceded in the surah of al-A'raf, in a way that suffices without repeating it here as well.

Ibn Kathir said: The safest course in this matter is the way of the early Muslims (al-salaf), which is to let pass what has come concerning it in the Book and the Sunnah, without modality (takyif), distortion (tahrif), likening (tashbih), denial (ta'til), or representation (tamthil).

We have already mentioned what the imams of modern astronomy (al-falak al-hadith) have established: that the Throne is a real, existing body, and that it is the center of all worlds, that is, the center of attraction, governance, influence, and order.

(p-4171) The discussion on the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:

[6] ﴿To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth and whatever is between them and whatever is under the soil.﴾

﴿To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth and whatever is between them and whatever is under the soil.﴾ This is an explanation of the comprehensiveness of His dominion (qahr) and sovereignty (malakah) over all things. That is: all of them are under His sovereignty, His domination, His authority (saltanah), and His influence. None of them exists, moves, rests, changes, or remains fixed except by His command.

Commentary on the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[7] ﴿And if you speak aloud, then indeed He knows the secret and what is yet more hidden.﴾

﴿And if you speak aloud, then indeed He knows the secret and what is yet more hidden.﴾ This is an explanation of the completeness of His subtle knowledge (lutf). That is: His knowledge penetrates everything. He knows its outward and inward aspects, the secret (al-sirr) and the secret of the secret (sirr al-sirr). Thus, whether you speak aloud or lower your voice, He knows it, whether it is loud or soft.

The discussion of the words of His Exalted saying:

[8] ﴿Allah! There is no god but He. To Him belong the Most Beautiful Names.﴾

﴿Allah﴾ means: that Revealer, described by these attributes, is Allah. ﴿There is no god but He. To Him belong the Most Beautiful Names﴾, i.e., the most excellent ones (al-Husna, "the most beautiful"), because they indicate meanings of sanctity, glorification, exaltation, lordship, and actions which are the utmost in beauty. And His saying, Exalted is He:

**The commentary on the words of Allah, the Exalted:**

[9–10] ﴿Has the story of Moses reached you?﴾ ﴿When he saw a fire and said to his family, "Stay here, for I have perceived a fire. Perhaps I will bring you a burning brand from it, or find at the fire some guidance."﴾ [Ta-Ha: 10].

﴿Has the story of Moses reached you?﴾ is either a continuation of the narrative or a new sentence (*isti'naf*, a resumptive sentence that begins a fresh topic). Its purpose is to establish the matter of monotheism (*tawhid*) with which the preceding verse ended, by showing that it is the call of every prophet, especially the most famous of them in report, Moses, peace be upon him. He was addressed with the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, I am Allah; there is no deity except Me﴾ [Ta-Ha: 14], and Allah concluded his account in this surah with the words: ﴿Your God is only Allah, other than whom there is no deity﴾ [Ta-Ha: 98]. Or it establishes the comprehensiveness of His clear knowledge, as in the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And if you speak aloud﴾ [Ta-Ha: 7], etc., and His words after it: ﴿He has encompassed all things in knowledge﴾ [Ta-Ha: 98], both of which are mentioned together. Or it urges the Prophet, may the blessings of Allah be upon him, to take Moses as an example in patience and steadfastness, because he was tested with something greater than this and was patient, and the final outcome was his.

At the beginning of the account of Moses, peace be upon him, the manner in which revelation began to him and Allah's speaking to him is indicated. This happened after Moses had completed the term that had been agreed between him and his father-in-law, in tending the sheep. He set out with his family heading for the land of Egypt, after his long absence from it, and with him was his wife. He lost the way. It was a wintry night, and he stopped at a place between ravines and mountains, in cold and winter. While he was in that state, he perceived a fire from the side of Mount Sinai (*al-Tur*), as Allah narrated it in His words: ﴿When he saw a fire and said to his family, "Stay here, for I have perceived a fire"﴾ [Ta-Ha: 10]. That is, I saw it with clear sight without any doubt. ﴿Perhaps I will bring you a burning brand from it﴾ [Ta-Ha: 10], that is, a kindled flame by which you may warm yourselves. ﴿Or find at the fire some guidance﴾ [Ta-Ha: 10], that is, a guide who will show me the way.

The discourse on the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[11] ﴿So when he came to it, he was called, "O Moses,"﴾ [12] ﴿"Indeed, I am your Lord, so take off your sandals. Indeed, you are in the sacred valley, Tuwa."﴾ [Ta-Ha: 11–12].

﴿So when he came to it﴾, i.e., the fire, ﴿he was called, "O Moses"﴾ ﴿"Indeed, I am your Lord, so take off your sandals. Indeed, you are in the sacred valley, Tuwa."﴾ [Ta-Ha: 12], meaning: therein it is incumbent to observe proper conduct (adab), by glorifying it and showing reverence for it, because the Truth manifests itself there, just as the etiquette of standing is observed before kings. (Tuwa): a proper noun for the valley.

(p-4173) On the interpretation of His words, may He be exalted:

[13] ﴿And I have chosen you, so listen to what is revealed.﴾ [14] ﴿Indeed, I am Allah; there is no deity except Me, so worship Me and establish prayer for My remembrance.﴾ [Ta-Ha: 14] [15] ﴿Indeed, the Hour is coming – I am almost concealing it – so that every soul may be recompensed for what it strives.﴾ [Ta-Ha: 15].

﴿And I have chosen you﴾, i.e., I have selected you for prophethood. ﴿So listen to what is revealed﴾, i.e., to that which is revealed, or to the revelation. Then He clarified it with His words: ﴿Indeed, I am Allah; there is no deity except Me, so worship Me﴾ [Ta-Ha: 14], i.e., single Me out for worship. ﴿And establish prayer for My remembrance﴾ [Ta-Ha: 14], i.e., that you remember Me in it with your heart, your tongue and all your limbs, by making its movements indicative of what is in the heart and the tongue. Abu al-Su'ud said: Prayer was singled out for mention and specified with the command to worship because of its excellence and eminence over the other acts of worship, given that it combines the remembrance of the One worshipped and the occupation of the heart and tongue with His remembrance. This is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿for My remembrance﴾ [Ta-Ha: 14], i.e., so that you remember Me, for My remembrance as it should be is not realized except within worship and prayer. Or [it means]: so that you remember Me in it, because it contains the invocations. Or [it means]: for My remembrance specifically, not mixed with the remembrance of other than Me. Or [it means]: for the sincere remembrance of Me and seeking My countenance, not showing off with it, and not intending with it any other aim. Or [it means]: so that you be one who remembers Me without forgetting. End of quote.

Then He indicated the obligation of singling Him out in worship and establishing prayer for His remembrance, by His saying: ﴿Indeed, the Hour is coming﴾ [Ta-Ha: 15], i.e., it will certainly occur without doubt: ﴿I am almost concealing it so that every soul may be recompensed for what it strives﴾ [Ta-Ha: 15], i.e., for its striving, chosen by itself. The lam is connected to ﴿coming﴾. Since the concealment of the Hour is among the certainties, and in (kada) there is a sense of nearness to that, because it is not established for definitively affirming the act, the scholars interpreted the verse in several ways:

The first: that (kada) from Him, exalted is He, is obligatory [i.e., certain]. The meaning is: I conceal it from the creation. Like His saying: ﴿Perhaps it will be near﴾ [al-Isra: 51], i.e., it is near.

The second: Abu Muslim said: (akadu) means "I intend," like His saying: ﴿Thus did We devise for Joseph﴾ [Yusuf: 76].

(p-4174) Among their commonly used proverbs: "I will not do that, nor do I intend (akad) to," i.e., nor do I want to do it. Al-Shihab said: Interpreting (akadu) as (uridu, "I want") is one of its meanings, as transmitted by Ibn Jinni in al-Muhtasib from al-Akhfash. They cited as evidence for it the verse:

"She almost, and I almost [desired], and that is the best of desires, if what passed of the idle play of passion would return."

meaning "she desired," due to his saying: "that is the best of desires."

The third: that (akadu) is a filler (silah) in the speech. Zayd al-Khayl said:

"Swift to the battle, bearing his weapon; and his opponent scarcely breathes."

The fourth: that the meaning is: I almost conceal it, so I do not mention it in general terms, nor do I say it is coming. This is due to the intensity of His, exalted is He, desire to conceal it. However, in mentioning it in general terms there is wisdom, namely kindness to the believers, to urge them toward righteous deeds, and to cut off the excuses of others, so that they cannot plead ignorance. There are other interpretations that are not free from strained reasoning, even though the wording allows them. And His saying, exalted is He:

(p-4173) On the interpretation of His words, may He be exalted:

[13] ﴿And I have chosen you, so listen to what is revealed.﴾ [14] ﴿Indeed, I am Allah; there is no deity except Me, so worship Me and establish prayer for My remembrance.﴾ [Ta-Ha: 14] [15] ﴿Indeed, the Hour is coming – I am almost concealing it – so that every soul may be recompensed for what it strives.﴾ [Ta-Ha: 15].

﴿And I have chosen you﴾, i.e., I have selected you for prophethood. ﴿So listen to what is revealed﴾, i.e., to that which is revealed, or to the revelation. Then He clarified it with His words: ﴿Indeed, I am Allah; there is no deity except Me, so worship Me﴾ [Ta-Ha: 14], i.e., single Me out for worship. ﴿And establish prayer for My remembrance﴾ [Ta-Ha: 14], i.e., that you remember Me in it with your heart, your tongue and all your limbs, by making its movements indicative of what is in the heart and the tongue. Abu al-Su'ud said: Prayer was singled out for mention and specified with the command to worship because of its excellence and eminence over the other acts of worship, given that it combines the remembrance of the One worshipped and the occupation of the heart and tongue with His remembrance. This is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿for My remembrance﴾ [Ta-Ha: 14], i.e., so that you remember Me, for My remembrance as it should be is not realized except within worship and prayer. Or [it means]: so that you remember Me in it, because it contains the invocations. Or [it means]: for My remembrance specifically, not mixed with the remembrance of other than Me. Or [it means]: for the sincere remembrance of Me and seeking My countenance, not showing off with it, and not intending with it any other aim. Or [it means]: so that you be one who remembers Me without forgetting. End of quote.

Then He indicated the obligation of singling Him out in worship and establishing prayer for His remembrance, by His saying: ﴿Indeed, the Hour is coming﴾ [Ta-Ha: 15], i.e., it will certainly occur without doubt: ﴿I am almost concealing it so that every soul may be recompensed for what it strives﴾ [Ta-Ha: 15], i.e., for its striving, chosen by itself. The lam is connected to ﴿coming﴾. Since the concealment of the Hour is among the certainties, and in (kada) there is a sense of nearness to that, because it is not established for definitively affirming the act, the scholars interpreted the verse in several ways:

The first: that (kada) from Him, exalted is He, is obligatory [i.e., certain]. The meaning is: I conceal it from the creation. Like His saying: ﴿Perhaps it will be near﴾ [al-Isra: 51], i.e., it is near.

The second: Abu Muslim said: (akadu) means "I intend," like His saying: ﴿Thus did We devise for Joseph﴾ [Yusuf: 76].

(p-4174) Among their commonly used proverbs: "I will not do that, nor do I intend (akad) to," i.e., nor do I want to do it. Al-Shihab said: Interpreting (akadu) as (uridu, "I want") is one of its meanings, as transmitted by Ibn Jinni in al-Muhtasib from al-Akhfash. They cited as evidence for it the verse:

"She almost, and I almost [desired], and that is the best of desires, if what passed of the idle play of passion would return."

meaning "she desired," due to his saying: "that is the best of desires."

The third: that (akadu) is a filler (silah) in the speech. Zayd al-Khayl said:

"Swift to the battle, bearing his weapon; and his opponent scarcely breathes."

The fourth: that the meaning is: I almost conceal it, so I do not mention it in general terms, nor do I say it is coming. This is due to the intensity of His, exalted is He, desire to conceal it. However, in mentioning it in general terms there is wisdom, namely kindness to the believers, to urge them toward righteous deeds, and to cut off the excuses of others, so that they cannot plead ignorance. There are other interpretations that are not free from strained reasoning, even though the wording allows them. And His saying, exalted is He:

The discussion on the interpretation of His saying:

[16] ﴿So let not one who does not believe in it and follows his desire turn you away from it, lest you perish.﴾

﴿So let not turn you away from it﴾ means: from affirming the Hour. ﴿One who does not believe in it and follows his desire﴾ means: what his self craves of appetites, and abandoning reflection and reasoning (istidlal). ﴿Lest you perish﴾ means: lest you be destroyed.

Al-Zamakhshari said: He means that those who do not believe in the Hereafter are the vast multitude, since nothing is more grievous to the disbelievers, nor do they deny anything more strongly, than resurrection. So let not the abundance of their rabble terrify you, nor the greatness of their numbers. Do not let the multitude make your foot slip. Know that they, although they are so numerous, have as their leader in what they are in desire and following it, not proof (burhan) and its study. In this there is a great exhortation to knowledge of the evidence (dalil), a forceful warning against taqlid (blind imitation of others without evidence), and a warning that destruction and perdition come with taqlid and its adherents. And His saying, exalted is He:

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 20, verses 17–18:

The discussion of His saying, the Exalted:

[17] ﴿And what is that in your right hand, O Moses?﴾ [18] ﴿He said, "It is my staff; I lean upon it, and I beat down leaves with it for my sheep, and I have other uses for it."﴾ [Ta-Ha: 18].

﴿And what is that in your right hand, O Moses?﴾ is the beginning of what Allah, the Exalted, is about to bestow upon him of the dazzling proof (burhan). In the question there is an awakening for him and an alert to the wonders of creation that are about to appear to him. ﴿He said, "It is my staff; I lean upon it﴾ [Ta-Ha: 18], i.e., I rely on it when I am exhausted, or when I stand at the head of the flock and at the time of the leap. ﴿And I beat down leaves with it for my sheep﴾ [Ta-Ha: 18], i.e., I strike the foliage with it and knock it down for them so they may eat it. ﴿And I have other uses for it﴾ [Ta-Ha: 18], i.e., other needs.

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 20, verses 22–23:

(p-4176) The discussion on the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[22] ﴿And draw your hand to your side; it will come out white without disease, as another sign,﴾ [23] ﴿That We may show you of Our greatest signs.﴾ [Ta-Ha: 22–23].

﴿And draw your hand to your side﴾ i.e., your armpit (ibt). ﴿It will come out white﴾ i.e., luminous. ﴿Without disease﴾ i.e., without ugliness or defect, like the whiteness of leprosy (baras), from which one recoils. Al-Zamakhshari (al-Zamakhshari) held that His saying, exalted is He, ﴿without disease﴾ is a euphemism for leprosy, just as the private part is referred to by "al-sau'a" (the shameful part). He said: Leprosy is the most hated thing to the Arabs, and they have a great aversion to it, and their ears recoil at its name. So it was fitting that it be referred to by a euphemism. You will not find any better, more subtle, or more effective for the joints than the euphemisms and courtesies of the Qur'an. End of quote. ﴿Another sign﴾ i.e., another miracle besides the staff. ﴿That We may show you of Our greatest signs﴾ [Ta-Ha: 23] is connected to an implied element that the noble context points to. That is: We showed you what We showed you now, although their proper place was to appear after the challenge and the disputation, so that We show you first some of Our greatest signs, and your heart may be strengthened to debate the tyrants. And His saying, exalted is He:

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 20, verse 24:

The discussion of His saying, exalted is He:

[24] ﴿Go to Pharaoh; indeed, he has transgressed.﴾

﴿Go to Pharaoh﴾ is a transition to what is the actual purpose, after preparing the preceding premises. It is separated from the commands before it (lit. "it is cut off from what precedes it of commands") to signal its importance. That is: go to him with the great signs you have seen, call him to worship Me, and warn him of My retribution. This was related by Abu al-Su'ud (Abu al-Su'ud, author of Irshad al-Aql al-Salim, a tafsir).

And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿indeed, he has transgressed﴾, meaning: he exceeded the limit in arrogance and insolence, to the point that he dared to lay claim to the great matter, which is the claim of lordship. Therefore it is necessary to alert him to his transgression through rational proofs, which the miracles have confirmed.

(p-٤١٧٧)The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[25] ﴿He said, "My Lord, expand for me my breast."﴾ [26] ﴿"And ease for me my task."﴾ [Ta-Ha: 26] [27] ﴿"And untie a knot from my tongue."﴾ [Ta-Ha: 27] [28] ﴿"That they may understand my speech."﴾ [Ta-Ha: 28].

﴿He said, "My Lord, expand for me my breast."﴾ ﴿"And ease for me my task."﴾ [Ta-Ha: 26] ﴿"And untie a knot from my tongue."﴾ [Ta-Ha: 27] ﴿"That they may understand my speech."﴾ [Ta-Ha: 28] He asked for that only because of what he feared from the people of Fir'awn (Pharaoh) concerning the man he had killed, and because of what he had been sent with: confronting a tyrannical, obstinate king, the most insolent of kings and the most extreme in rebellion and disbelief, which necessitates a Lordly care. Then, peace be upon him, asked his Lord that He strengthen him with his brother Aaron, so that he would be a supporter for him and would speak on his behalf about much of what his tongue does not express clearly, by his saying:

[36] He said: "You have been given your request, O Moses." [37] "And We had already bestowed favour upon you another time."

He said, "You have been given your request, O Moses" — i.e., your supplication has been answered.

And His saying, "And We had already bestowed favour upon you another time" [20:37] is a resumed statement (kalam mustanaf), brought to confirm what precedes it and to increase the tranquillity of Moses's soul in accepting it, by showing that God, who bestowed upon him those complete blessings without any prior supplication or request from him, is all the more fit and worthy to bestow upon him the like of them when he is asking and calling upon Him. And the opening of it with an oath (qasam) is for the complete care given to this matter. This was conveyed by Abu al-Su'ud.

And His saying, "another time" [20:37] means: at another time.

[38] ﴿When We inspired in your mother what is inspired.﴾ [39] ﴿Saying, "Put him into the chest, then cast it into the river, and let the river throw it onto the bank, where an enemy of Mine and an enemy of his will take him." And I bestowed upon you love from Me, so that you would be raised under My eye.﴾ [Ta-Ha: 39].

﴿When We inspired﴾, i.e., We cast [the thought] through inspiration (*ilham*): ﴿in your mother what is inspired﴾. ﴿Put him into the chest﴾ [Ta-Ha: 39], i.e., the box. ﴿Then cast it into the river﴾ [Ta-Ha: 39], i.e., the sea, relying upon its Creator. ﴿Let the river throw it onto the bank, where an enemy of Mine﴾ [Ta-Ha: 39], because of his claim to divinity, ﴿and an enemy of his﴾ [Ta-Ha: 39], because of his call to abandon what he claims.

Al-Zamakhshari (*al-Zamakhshari*) said: Since the will and decree of God, exalted is He, ensured that the course of the river would not fail to bring the child to the bank and cast him there, He followed the path of metaphor (*majaz*) and treated the river as if it were a discerning being that had been commanded, so that it would obey the command and carry out its decree. Thus it is said: ﴿let the river throw it onto the bank﴾ [Ta-Ha: 39], i.e., by way of implicit metaphor (*isti'ara bil-kinaya*), by likening the river to a commanded and obedient subject. The attribution of command is imaginative depiction (*takhyil*). His words, exalted is He: ﴿And I bestowed upon you love from Me﴾ [Ta-Ha: 39], i.e., love coming from Me, which I planted in the hearts of those who saw you; for this reason Pharaoh loved you. ﴿So that you would be raised under My eye﴾ [Ta-Ha: 39], i.e., so that you would be nurtured in the hand of the enemy, under My watch, with protection and care. Thus, ﴿under My eye﴾ (*'ala 'aini*) is a representational metaphor (*isti'ara tamthiliyya*) for protection and safeguarding, because what is protected is placed within sight. It has been said that ﴿'ala﴾ (upon) here carries the meaning of ﴿bi﴾ (with), because originally it means "within my sight" (*bi-mar'an minni*).

Discourse on the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:

[40] ﴿When your sister walked along and said, "Shall I direct you to one who will take charge of him?" So We returned you to your mother that her eye might be cooled and she would not grieve. And you killed a soul, but We saved you from distress and tested you with a [severe] testing. Then you remained for years among the people of Madyan. Then you came [here] at a decreed time, O Moses.﴾

﴿When your sister walked along and said, "Shall I direct you to one who will take charge of him?"﴾ That is: who will undertake to nurse and rear him.

(p-4180) So they accepted her proposal. This was because, when he had settled among the household of Pharaoh, they offered him wet-nurses, but he refused them, as God the Exalted says: ﴿And We had forbidden him the wet-nurses﴾ [al-Qasas: 12]. So his sister came and said: ﴿Shall I direct you to a household who will rear him for you while they are sincere toward him?﴾ [al-Qasas: 12], and she brought his mother, as He said: ﴿So We returned you to your mother﴾, that is, even though you were in the hand of the enemy: ﴿that her eye might be cooled﴾, that is, by seeing you; ﴿and she would not grieve﴾, that is, over your separation. These are favors added to his deliverance from being killed.

Then He pointed to what He had bestowed upon him by way of deliverance from killing, which cannot be averted by deception, through His words: ﴿And you killed a soul﴾, that is, one of Pharaoh's people, namely the Copt whom the Israelite sought help against, so Moses struck him and dispatched him. That is, you were distressed over the retaliation: ﴿so We saved you from distress﴾, that is, the distress of killing, by turning away from you what you feared. This is because he, peace be upon him, fled from Pharaoh's people until he reached the water of Madyan, and that righteous man said to him: ﴿Fear not; you have escaped from the wrongdoing people﴾ [al-Qasas: 25]. ﴿And We tested you with a [severe] testing﴾, that is: We put you to trial with a trial. Here "futun" may be a verbal noun like "shukur," or types of trials, taking it as the plural of "fitnah," meaning: We made for you a relief and a way out from them. This is a summary of what has been mentioned before.

﴿Then you remained for years among the people of Madyan﴾, that is: honored in standing and provided for, in the company of the most pious and righteous of their men, who was their prophet, peace be upon him. ﴿Then you came [here] at a decreed time, O Moses﴾, that is: after you had fulfilled the term fixed between you and Shu'ayb as wages, you came with your family in accordance with what had preceded in My decree and My destiny, that I should speak to you and make you a prophet at a time which I had appointed for that purpose. You came only at that measure, neither ahead of it nor behind it. The command belongs to Him, exalted is He, who directs His servants and creation as He wills.

Abu al-Su'ud said: His words, exalted is He, ﴿O Moses﴾ are an honoring of him, peace be upon him, and an indication that the narrative has ended, which is the detailed account of the other occasion that occurred before the occasion mentioned first.

"Allah's words:

The discussion on the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:

[41] ﴿And I have chosen you for Myself﴾ [42] ﴿Go, you and your brother, with My signs, and do not slacken in remembering Me﴾ [Ta-Ha: 42].

﴿And I have chosen you for Myself﴾ is a reminder of His words, exalted is He: ﴿And I have chosen you﴾ [Ta-Ha: 13], and a preparation for his (peace be upon him) being sent to Pharaoh, supported by his brother. The word (al-istina'," from the form "iftiʿal" of (al-sun'," meaning a favour (sanii'ah). It is said: the prince "istana'a" so-and-so for himself, meaning he made him an object of his honour by his choice and by bringing him near to himself, by making him one of his special companions and boon-companions. Thus the meaning is borrowed through a metaphorical image (istiʿarah tamthiliyyah) from that meaning, the likened (al-mushabbah bihi) to the likened (al-mushabbah), namely, making him a noble prophet, a speaker with God, one upon whom great blessings were bestowed.

Abu al-Su'ud said: the shift away from the plural of majesty (nun al-'azamah) occurring in His words, exalted is He: ﴿And We tested you﴾ [Ta-Ha: 40] and its two preceding parallels, is a preparation for the singular use of the word (al-nafs, "self"), which suits the context, for it is more effective in establishing the meaning of (al-istina') and (al-istikhlas, "selection"). Then He clarified what is intended by (al-istina') by His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿Go, you and your brother, with My signs﴾ [Ta-Ha: 42], i.e., with My miracles, such as the staff, the whiteness of the hand, and the loosening of the knot, together with what He granted him as support in his hand. ﴿And do not slacken in remembering Me﴾ [Ta-Ha: 42], i.e., do not falter or fall short in remembering Me with what befits Me of sublime attributes, when conveying My message and calling to Me."

Commentary on the interpretation of His words, Exalted is He:

[43] ﴿Go, you two, to Pharaoh; indeed, he has transgressed.﴾ [44] ﴿And speak to him with gentle speech, perhaps he will be reminded or fear.﴾ [Ta-Ha: 44]

﴿Go, you two, to Pharaoh; indeed, he has transgressed.﴾ ﴿And speak to him with gentle speech, perhaps he will be reminded or fear.﴾ [Ta-Ha: 44] That is: My punishment. For gentle speech breaks the obstinacy of the stubborn and softens the disposition of the tyrants. This is explained in His words, Exalted is He: ﴿So say, "Would you like to purify yourself?"﴾ [An-Nazi'at: 18] ﴿and I will guide you to your Lord, so you would fear Him.﴾ [An-Nazi'at: 19] And in a similar manner (p-4182) our Prophet, may the blessings of Allah be upon him, was commanded in His words: ﴿Invite to the way of your Lord with wisdom and good instruction, and argue with them in the best manner.﴾ [An-Nahl: 125] It is evident that the hope expressed in (perhaps, la'alla) comes from the two of them, not from Allah, for that is not valid from Him. Therefore al-Qadi said: That is, proceed with the matter in your hope and expectation that it will bear fruit, and We will not disappoint your effort. For the one who hopes is striving, while the one who despairs is merely going through the motions. The benefit in sending them and in urging them to exert effort, even though He knows that he will not believe, is to establish the proof, cut off excuses, and manifest the signs that occurred in the course of that.

Commentary on the interpretation of His words, Exalted is He:

[45] ﴿They said, "Our Lord, indeed we fear that he will hasten against us [with punishment] or that he will transgress."﴾ [46] ﴿He said, "Fear not. Indeed, I am with you both; I hear and I see."﴾ [Ta-Ha: 45–46].

﴿They said, "Our Lord, indeed we fear that he will hasten against us"﴾ meaning: that he will anticipate us with punishment. ﴿or that he will transgress﴾ meaning: that he will increase in tyranny through obstinacy in rejecting our proofs, then order our killing, or go beyond the limit to say about Your matter what is not fitting, because of his audacity and the hardness of his heart. Al-Zamakhshari confined himself to the second [meaning]. He noted that bringing it in this unrestricted form, and by way of allusion, contains a door of good manners and an avoidance of uttering the grave matter.

﴿He said, "Fear not"﴾ [Ta-Ha: 46], meaning: from his excess and tyranny. ﴿Indeed, I am with you both﴾ [Ta-Ha: 46], meaning: with protection and support. ﴿I hear and I see﴾ [Ta-Ha: 46], meaning: what passes between you both and him. So I watch over you both with protection. The object is omitted for the indication (of context), or it has been made to take the place of an intransitive verb, completing what protection by itself suffices for. As if it were said: "I am your Protector and Helper, Hearing and Seeing." And when the Protector is such, protection and support are complete, and concern for the enemy departs.

The Interpretation of His Words, Exalted is He:

[47] ﴿So go to him and say: "Indeed we are two messengers of your Lord, so send with us the Children of Israel and do not torment them. We have certainly come to you with a sign from your Lord. And peace be upon whoever follows guidance."﴾

﴿So go to him and say: "Indeed we are two messengers of your Lord, so send with us the Children of Israel"﴾ That is: by releasing them from captivity and servitude, and letting them go with us to our homeland, Palestine. ﴿And do not torment them﴾ That is: by leaving them in the state of forced labour and humiliation in arduous tasks in which they are. ﴿We have certainly come to you with a sign from your Lord﴾ That is: the truth of my messengership to you is established from Him, Exalted is He, by this. ﴿And peace be upon whoever follows guidance﴾ That is: whoever believes in the clear signs of Allah that manifest the truth. And in this, in the most gentle manner, is an encouragement to follow the two of them, which is not hidden.

The discussion of the Almighty's words:

[48] ﴿Indeed, it has been revealed to us that the punishment is for whoever denies and turns away.﴾

﴿Indeed, it has been revealed to us﴾, i.e., from our Lord. ﴿That the punishment is for whoever denies﴾, i.e., His signs, exalted is He. ﴿And turns away﴾, i.e., turns away from them. In it there is a gentleness in the warning beyond which there is nothing more, in that it does not explicitly state that the punishment will descend upon him.

The discussion of the interpretation of His words, Exalted is He:

[49] ﴿He said, "So who is your Lord, O Moses?"﴾ [50] ﴿He said, "Our Lord is He who gave everything its creation and then guided it."﴾ [Ta-Ha: 49–50].

﴿He said﴾, i.e., Pharaoh: ﴿"So who is your Lord, O Moses?"﴾ ﴿He said, "Our Lord is He who gave everything its creation and then guided it."﴾ [Ta-Ha: 50], i.e., He bestowed upon every thing among human souls its form and shape, which corresponds to the benefit assigned to it, so He fashioned it accordingly and proportioned it, then He guided it by bestowing upon it the intellect (ʿaql) that distinguishes between good and evil. (p-4184) The meaning of this verse is like the verse: ﴿And a soul and He who proportioned it﴾ [ash-Shams: 7], ﴿and inspired it with its wickedness and its righteousness﴾ [ash-Shams: 8], and the verse: ﴿And We guided him to the two paths﴾ [al-Balad: 10].

The Exposition of the Meaning of the Qur'an (Ta'wil, interpretation) on His saying, may He be exalted:

[51] ﴿He said, "Then what is the state of the earlier generations?"﴾ [52] ﴿He said, "Their knowledge is with my Lord, in a Record. My Lord neither errs nor forgets."﴾ [Ta-Ha: 52].

﴿He said﴾, i.e., Pharaoh: ﴿"Then what is the state of the earlier generations?"﴾ ﴿He said, "Their knowledge is with my Lord, in a Record. My Lord neither errs nor forgets."﴾ [Ta-Ha: 52], i.e., what is the condition of the bygone generations, and what befell them? This question was either to divert Musa (peace be upon him) from what he was calling to before his council (mala'), and to occupy him with what does not concern the message he was sent with, or because of the assumption that the Messenger knows the unseen, so he wanted to learn the report of what had passed and open a door for refutation and denial, through obstinacy and contentiousness. Musa (peace be upon him) answered him that this is a question about the unseen, which Allah has reserved for Himself, so none knows it but Him, and it is not part of the function of prophethood. Rather, its knowledge is written in the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz), counted and not forgotten.

It is also permissible that ﴿in a Record﴾ be a figurative expression (tamthil) for its firm establishment and fixity in the knowledge of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, in that He has entrusted it to the Knowing One and recorded it with scribes. Al-Qadi said in al-'Inayah: so He likens His knowledge, exalted is He, to a firm knowledge that does not change, to one who knows something and writes it in his register so that it does not disappear at all. Thus His saying ﴿My Lord neither errs nor forgets﴾ [Ta-Ha: 52] serves as tarshih (an elaboration that completes the figure of speech) for the analogy, and also as ihtiras (a safeguard against misunderstanding), because one who does such a thing does it out of fear of forgetting, and Allah, exalted is He, is far above that.

Thus the word al-Kitab (the Record), on this reading, retains its linguistic meaning, which is the register (daftar), not the Preserved Tablet.

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 20, verse 53:

Concerning the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[53] ﴿Who has made for you the earth a cradle, and threaded for you therein roads, and sent down from the sky water, and We brought forth thereby pairs of various plants.﴾

﴿Who has made for you the earth a cradle﴾, i.e., a bed (firash). ﴿And threaded for you therein roads, and sent down from the sky water, and We brought forth thereby pairs of various plants﴾, i.e., kinds of plants of differing species, in taste, smell, form and benefit.

A subtle point:

Al-Zamakhshari (d. 538 AH) considered His saying, ﴿We brought forth﴾, to be an instance of iltifat (shift of grammatical person). Al-Nasir (Ibn al-Munayyir) criticized him, saying: iltifat occurs only in the speech of a single speaker who varies his discourse in various ways, and what we are dealing with is not like that. For Allah, exalted is He, related of Musa, peace be upon him, his saying to Pharaoh: ﴿Its knowledge is with my Lord, in a Book. My Lord neither errs nor forgets﴾ [Ta-Ha: 52], then his saying: ﴿Who has made for you the earth a cradle﴾ up to his saying: ﴿We brought forth thereby pairs of various plants﴾. So either this is said by Musa, in which case it belongs to the type of the speech of the king's close attendants, "We have commanded and we have built up," when they mean the king, and this is not iltifat. Or the speech of Musa ended at His saying: ﴿nor forgets﴾ [Ta-Ha: 52], and then Allah, exalted is He, began describing His own essence with attributes of His bounty toward His creation, so this is not iltifat either. Rather it is a transition from narration to the composition of direct address. On this interpretation, the reader should pause briefly at His saying: ﴿nor forgets﴾ [Ta-Ha: 52], so that the narration comes to rest at its end.

It admits another possibility: that Musa described Allah, exalted is He, with these attributes using the third-person form, saying: ﴿Who has made for you the earth a cradle, and threaded for you therein roads, and sent down from the sky water, and We brought forth thereby pairs of various plants﴾. Then, when Allah, exalted is He, related it from him, He attributed the pronoun to His own essence, because the one relating is the one related in Musa's speech. Thus the referent of the two pronouns is one. This view is a good one with a delicate margin, and it is the closest of the views to iltifat. However, al-Zamakhshari did not intend it. And Allah knows best. The speech of al-Nasir has ended.

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 20, verse 54–55:

And His saying, exalted is He:

Discussion on the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[54] ﴿Eat and graze your livestock. Indeed, in that are signs for those of intellect.﴾ [55] ﴿From it We created you, and into it We will return you, and from it We will bring you forth once more.﴾ [Ta-Ha: 55].

On the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[61] ﴿Moses said to them, "Woe to you! Do not fabricate a lie against God, lest He destroy you with a punishment. Indeed, whoever fabricates has failed."﴾ [62] ﴿So they disputed among themselves about their affair and kept their private counsel secret.﴾ [Ta-Ha: 62] [63] ﴿They said, "Indeed, these two are magicians who want to expel you from your land with their magic and do away with your most excellent way of life."﴾ [Ta-Ha: 63].

﴿Moses said to them﴾, that is, offering them sincere counsel and warning, so that their excuse would be cut off: ﴿Woe to you! Do not fabricate a lie against God﴾, that is, do not make people imagine, through your deeds, the bringing into being of things that have no realities, and that they are created when they are not created. Then you would have lied against God, exalted is He. ﴿Lest He destroy you﴾, that is, uproot you, ﴿with a punishment﴾, that is, a terrible one, because of His anger against you. ﴿And indeed, whoever fabricates has failed.﴾ ﴿So they disputed among themselves about their affair and kept their private counsel secret﴾ [Ta-Ha: 62]. ﴿They said﴾ [Ta-Ha: 63], that is, by way of secret consultation and concealment: ﴿Indeed, these two are magicians who want to expel you from your land with their magic and do away with your most excellent way of life﴾ [Ta-Ha: 63], that is, your most excellent path (p-4188). This is what they were upon. They mean that the aim of Moses and Aaron is to depose Pharaoh from his kingship, by making him a slave to another, and to establish themselves in his place, and to make their people in your place, and to compel you to leave your land and to nullify your way of life through their magic, with which they want to overpower you. And "al-muthla" is the feminine of "al-amthal," meaning "al-afdal" (the best). Their claim is this, because "every faction rejoices in what it has" (cf. Qur'an 23:53).

A subtle point:

Regarding His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, these two are magicians﴾ [Ta-Ha: 63], there are several readings:

The first: "Inna hadhayni la-sahiran" with the nun of "inna" doubled and "hadhayni" with a yāʾ, which is the reading of Abu ʿAmr. It follows the well-known practice of the operation of "inna" (the emphatic particle that governs the accusative).

The second: ﴿In hadhani la-sahiran﴾ [Ta-Ha: 63], with "in" lightened and rendered inoperative, as is most common with it when it is lightened. What follows it is nominative, as subject and predicate. The lām is the lām of the beginning (lām al-ibtidāʾ), to distinguish it from the negative particle. The Kufans hold that this lām here has the sense of "illa" (except), and that "in" before it is negative. They cited for the coming of the lām in the sense of exception the verse:

"Yesterday Aban was humbled after his might, and Aban was not [more] for the black foreigners."

The third: ﴿Inna hadhani la-sahiran﴾ [Ta-Ha: 63] with "inna" doubled and "hadhani" with an alif. It has been explained in several ways:

The first: its conformity with the dialect of those who use the alif in the dual in all its cases. They are the Banu al-Harith ibn Kaʿb, Khathʿam, Zubayd, Kinana, and others. One of them said:

"He took from us, between his ears, a stab."

And another said:

"Indeed her father and her father's father have reached the furthest point of glory."

(p-4189) The second: that "inna" here means "naʿam" (yes). Al-Mubarrad related this, citing the verse of the rajaz poet:

"O ʿUmar of goodness, may you be rewarded with Paradise; clothe my children and their mother."

"And say to them: 'Inna, inna-hu!' I swear by God that you will surely do it."

And the saying of ʿAbd Allah ibn Qays al-Ruqayyat:

"And they say: 'Grey hair has risen upon you,' and you have grown old, so I said: 'Inna-hu.'"

Abu ʿAli al-Farisi refuted al-Mubarrad, saying that nothing preceding had been answered by "naʿam." Al-Shamanni answered that their mutual disputing and secret counsel implies that some of them were asking others, so it is an answer to an implicit question. But this is far-fetched, for their secret counsel among themselves was not an inquiry about whether the two were magicians; rather they had already decided upon magic, saying: ﴿Have you come to us to expel us from our land with your magic?﴾ [Ta-Ha: 57], and then they kept secret counsel about what would overcome Moses. Unless it is said that the point of the answer is His saying: ﴿So gather your scheme﴾ [Ta-Ha: 64] etc., and what precedes it is a preparation. Al-Mughni has rejected this interpretation, since the occurrence of "naʿam" is rare to the point that some have denied it. Al-Damamini prohibited it, saying that Sibawayh and the masters related it from the eloquent Arabs. Accordingly, the lām in ﴿la-sahiran﴾ [Ta-Ha: 63] is the lām of the beginning, shifted to the predicate. The Basrans refused its entry upon the predicate and claimed that in such cases it enters upon an omitted subject, or is extra, or entered together with "inna" which means "naʿam," because of its resemblance to the emphatic particle in form.

I say: this is strained, and the evidences for the attachment of the predicate with the lām are numerous.

(p-4190) The third: since the case-ending does not appear in the singular, which is "hadha," it was made likewise in the dual, so that the dual would be like the singular, since it is derived from it. This view was chosen by the eminent scholar Taqi al-Din Abu al-ʿAbbas Ahmad ibn Taymiyya, may God have mercy on him, who claimed that the indeclinable form of the dual, when its singular is indeclinable, is more eloquent than its inflection. He said: more than one of the skilled grammarians has been aware of this. Then he raised two objections:

The first: that the seven readers agreed on the yāʾ in His saying: ﴿one of these two daughters of mine﴾ [al-Qasas: 27], although "hatayn" is the dual of "hata," which is indeclinable.

The second: that "alladhi" is indeclinable, yet they used "alladhayni" in the genitive and accusative. This is the language of the Qur'an, as in His saying: ﴿Our Lord, show us those who led us astray﴾ [Fussilat: 29]. He answered the first that "hatayn" came with the yāʾ according to the inflected dialect because of the harmony with "ibnatayya," and said: so inflection here is more eloquent than indeclinability, for the sake of harmony, just as indeclinability in ﴿Indeed these two are magicians﴾ [Ta-Ha: 63] is more eloquent than inflection, for the sake of harmony of the alif in "hadhani" with the alif in "sahiran." He answered the second by distinguishing between "alladhani" and "hadhani": "alladhani" is the dual of a triliteral noun, so it resembles "al-Zaydani," whereas "hadhani" is the dual of a noun of two letters, so it is firmly indeclinable, resembling particles. He, may God have mercy on him, said: some people claimed that the reading of one who reads ﴿Indeed these two﴾ [Ta-Ha: 63] is a grammatical error, and that ʿUthman, may God be pleased with him, said: "There is a grammatical error in the Mushaf, and the Arabs will set it right with their tongues." This report is false and not sound, for several reasons.

The first: the Companions used to hasten to denounce even the least of wrongs, so how would they permit a grammatical error in the Qur'an when there is no difficulty for them in removing it?

The second: the Arabs found grammatical error extremely repugnant in speech, so how would they not find its remaining in the Mushaf repugnant?

(p-4191) The third: the argument that the Arabs will set it right with their tongues is not valid, because the honored Mushaf is read by both Arab and non-Arab.

The fourth: it is established in the authentic reports that Zayd ibn Thabit wanted to write "al-tabut" with a hāʾ according to the dialect of the Ansar, but they prevented him from that and referred it to ʿUthman, may God be pleased with them. He ordered them to write it with a tāʾ according to the dialect of Quraysh. When it reached ʿUmar, may God be pleased with him, that Ibn Masʿud, may God be pleased with him, recited "ʿatta hin" according to the dialect of Hudhayl, he denounced that and said: "Teach the people in the dialect of Quraysh, for God revealed it only in their dialect, and did not reveal it in the dialect of Hudhayl." The words of Taqi al-Din end here, summarized.

This is the essence of what is in al-Mughni, al-Shudhur and their commentaries. There are other aspects of the verse which the lengthier works have explored at length, and what we have mentioned is the most delicate of them. And His saying, exalted is He:

"Indeed her father and her father's father have reached the furthest point of glory."

(p-4189) The second: that "inna" here means "naʿam" (yes). Al-Mubarrad related this, citing the verse of the rajaz poet:

"O ʿUmar of goodness, may you be rewarded with Paradise; clothe my children and their mother."

"And say to them: 'Inna, inna-hu!' I swear by God that you will surely do it."

And the saying of ʿAbd Allah ibn Qays al-Ruqayyat:

"And they say: 'Grey hair has risen upon you,' and you have grown old, so I said: 'Inna-hu.'"

Abu ʿAli al-Farisi refuted al-Mubarrad, saying that nothing preceding had been answered by "naʿam." Al-Shamanni answered that their mutual disputing and secret counsel implies that some of them were asking others, so it is an answer to an implicit question. But this is far-fetched, for their secret counsel among themselves was not an inquiry about whether the two were magicians; rather they had already decided upon magic, saying: ﴿Have you come to us to expel us from our land with your magic?﴾ [Ta-Ha: 57], and then they kept secret counsel about what would overcome Moses. Unless it is said that the point of the answer is His saying: ﴿So gather your scheme﴾ [Ta-Ha: 64] etc., and what precedes it is a preparation. Al-Mughni has rejected this interpretation, since the occurrence of "naʿam" is rare to the point that some have denied it. Al-Damamini prohibited it, saying that Sibawayh and the masters related it from the eloquent Arabs. Accordingly, the lām in ﴿la-sahiran﴾ [Ta-Ha: 63] is the lām of the beginning, shifted to the predicate. The Basrans refused its entry upon the predicate and claimed that in such cases it enters upon an omitted subject, or is extra, or entered together with "inna" which means "naʿam," because of its resemblance to the emphatic particle in form.

I say: this is strained, and the evidences for the attachment of the predicate with the lām are numerous.

(p-4190) The third: since the case-ending does not appear in the singular, which is "hadha," it was made likewise in the dual, so that the dual would be like the singular, since it is derived from it. This view was chosen by the eminent scholar Taqi al-Din Abu al-ʿAbbas Ahmad ibn Taymiyya, may God have mercy on him, who claimed that the indeclinable form of the dual, when its singular is indeclinable, is more eloquent than its inflection. He said: more than one of the skilled grammarians has been aware of this. Then he raised two objections:

The first: that the seven readers agreed on the yāʾ in His saying: ﴿one of these two daughters of mine﴾ [al-Qasas: 27], although "hatayn" is the dual of "hata," which is indeclinable.

The second: that "alladhi" is indeclinable, yet they used "alladhayni" in the genitive and accusative. This is the language of the Qur'an, as in His saying: ﴿Our Lord, show us those who led us astray﴾ [Fussilat: 29]. He answered the first that "hatayn" came with the yāʾ according to the inflected dialect because of the harmony with "ibnatayya," and said: so inflection here is more eloquent than indeclinability, for the sake of harmony, just as indeclinability in ﴿Indeed these two are magicians﴾ [Ta-Ha: 63] is more eloquent than inflection, for the sake of harmony of the alif in "hadhani" with the alif in "sahiran." He answered the second by distinguishing between "alladhani" and "hadhani": "alladhani" is the dual of a triliteral noun, so it resembles "al-Zaydani," whereas "hadhani" is the dual of a noun of two letters, so it is firmly indeclinable, resembling particles. He, may God have mercy on him, said: some people claimed that the reading of one who reads ﴿Indeed these two﴾ [Ta-Ha: 63] is a grammatical error, and that ʿUthman, may God be pleased with him, said: "There is a grammatical error in the Mushaf, and the Arabs will set it right with their tongues." This report is false and not sound, for several reasons.

The first: the Companions used to hasten to denounce even the least of wrongs, so how would they permit a grammatical error in the Qur'an when there is no difficulty for them in removing it?

The second: the Arabs found grammatical error extremely repugnant in speech, so how would they not find its remaining in the Mushaf repugnant?

(p-4191) The third: the argument that the Arabs will set it right with their tongues is not valid, because the honored Mushaf is read by both Arab and non-Arab.

The fourth: it is established in the authentic reports that Zayd ibn Thabit wanted to write "al-tabut" with a hāʾ according to the dialect of the Ansar, but they prevented him from that and referred it to ʿUthman, may God be pleased with them. He ordered them to write it with a tāʾ according to the dialect of Quraysh. When it reached ʿUmar, may God be pleased with him, that Ibn Masʿud, may God be pleased with him, recited "ʿatta hin" according to the dialect of Hudhayl, he denounced that and said: "Teach the people in the dialect of Quraysh, for God revealed it only in their dialect, and did not reveal it in the dialect of Hudhayl." The words of Taqi al-Din end here, summarized.

This is the essence of what is in al-Mughni, al-Shudhur and their commentaries. There are other aspects of the verse which the lengthier works have explored at length, and what we have mentioned is the most delicate of them. And His saying, exalted is He:

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 20, verse 64:

The discussion of His saying, exalted is He:

[64] ﴿So gather your plot, then come in ranks, and whoever prevails today will have succeeded.﴾

﴿So gather your plot﴾ is an explicit statement of the objective, following the preliminary premises. The fa' (al-fa' al-fasihah, the "eloquent fa'," introducing an implied condition) indicates: that is, if the matter is as has been mentioned, namely that the two of them are sorcerers who intend to drive you out and remove you as has been stated, then resolve upon your plot and make it a unified decision, such that not one of you holds back from it. This is what Abu al-Su'ud stated. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿then come in ranks﴾ means lined up in formation, so that it would be more awe-inspiring in the hearts of those who see it. ﴿And whoever prevails﴾ means who gains the great favors from Pharaoh and his chiefs. ﴿today will have succeeded﴾ means who rises above and overcomes.

Subtleties:

From (al-Kashshaf) and its marginal notes by (al-Nasir).

The first: In giving the magicians the choice between casting first and Moses casting first, there is the employment of good manners toward him, humility before him, and lowering of the wing. It also indicates their giving fairness from themselves. It is as though Allah, Mighty and Exalted, inspired them with this, and taught Moses, may the blessings of Allah be upon him, to choose that they cast first, together with what it contains of answering courtesy with courtesy, so that they would bring out whatever stratagems of magic they had, and exhaust their utmost methods and effort. When they did so, Allah manifested His authority, hurled the truth upon falsehood so that it crushed it, and empowered the miracle over the magic so that it annihilated it, and it became a luminous sign for the observers and a clear lesson for those who take heed. Before that, they had shown courtesy toward him by their saying: ﴿So set between us and you an appointment which we will not fail to keep﴾ [Ta-Ha: 58], so they delegated the setting of the appointment to him. And just as Allah, Mighty and Majestic, inspired Moses here to make them begin with what they had, so that his casting of the staff afterward would be a hurling of the truth upon falsehood, which crushes it so that it vanishes, likewise He inspired him from the outset to make their appointment the day of their adornment and festival, so that the truth would be clear before the assembled witnesses, and thus more disgraceful to their scheming and more exposing of the veil of their sanctuary.

The second: Regarding the choice of His words, ﴿what is in your right hand﴾ [Ta-Ha: 69] over "your staff," two aspects are permitted:

One: that it be an exaltation of it, i.e., do not be concerned with these large, numerous bodies; for in your right hand is something greater than all of them, and these, despite their multitude, are the least and most insignificant thing in his sight. So cast it, and it will swallow them by Allah's permission and annihilate them.

The second: that it be a diminution of them, i.e., do not be troubled by the multitude of their ropes and staffs, and cast the small single stick of little body that is in your right hand. For by Allah's power it will swallow them, in its singularity and their multiplicity, in its smallness and their greatness. The purpose of belittling it in comparison with power is to belittle the magicians' scheming by way of a fortiori reasoning: for if it is greater in might while being insignificant in comparison with the power of Allah, the Exalted, then what is to be thought of their scheming, when this insignificant, meagre thing has swallowed it?

Rhetoricians have a method of elevating praise by exalting the army of the one praised's enemy, so that from this there follows the exaltation of the army of the one praised, who has overcome it and prevailed over it. Thus Allah diminished the matter of the staff, so that from it there follows the vanishing of the magicians' scheming, which was refuted by it in the twinkling of an eye.

Know that there must be a nuance that suits both matters, the exaltation and the diminution; and that, Allah knows best, is the intention of the referent in an indefinite manner, because ﴿what is in your right hand﴾ [Ta-Ha: 69] is more indefinite than "your staff." The Arabs have a manner of using indefiniteness, ambiguity and generality, which they adopt at times to belittle the matter they leave vague, and that it is, in the speaker's estimation, too minor to be singled out and clarified; and at other times to exalt its matter, and to indicate that it holds a place of concern for speaker and hearer alike, to the extent that it suffices by way of allusion and indication. This is the aspect in which it is granted both together.

Then al-Nasir said: In my view there is an aspect in the verse other than the purpose of exaltation and diminution. Allah knows best. It is that Moses, peace be upon him, when he first knew that the staff was a sign from Allah, Exalted, when He asked him about it with His words, ﴿And what is that in your right hand, O Moses?﴾ [Ta-Ha: 17], then Allah, Exalted, showed him its sign. When the time came for the need of the sign's manifestation through it, Allah, Exalted, said: ﴿And cast what is in your right hand﴾ [Ta-Ha: 69], so that he would be alerted by this formula to the moment when Allah, Exalted, had said to him: ﴿And what is that in your right hand?﴾ [Ta-Ha: 17], and He had shown him its sign. This would be an alert and a reassurance to him, since he was addressed with what he was accustomed to being addressed with at the time of the manifestation of its sign. That is a station suited to reassurance and steadfastness. Do you not see His words, Exalted: ﴿So Moses sensed fear within himself﴾ [Ta-Ha: 67]? End.

Abu Hayyan has another subtlety: what is in the right hand carries an indication of blessing and barakah. It cannot be said that in Surat al-A'raf it came: ﴿Cast your staff﴾ [al-A'raf: 117], and the story is one; because it is answered that the wording there prevents the observance of this nuance in what occurred here, and that it is a report of what came in meaning.

Thereupon al-Shihab al-Khafaji said: In what they mentioned there is scrutiny, because it is only complete if the address was in an Arabic wording or one synonymous with it, in which the same applies. The first is contrary to what actually occurred, and the second is far beyond reach, so reflect.

I say: The second was deemed unlikely only because of the assumption that there is no eloquence or subtle nuances except in the Arabic language. Yet the matter is not so. In that case the second is determined, and it is evident. And by it those subtleties are recovered.

Then He mentioned His blessings upon the Children of Israel and His great favours, and what He enjoined upon them of guarding gratitude for them, and warned them against exposing themselves to His wrath through disbelief in them, by His saying, glorified is He:

Discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[80] ﴿O Children of Israel, We had certainly delivered you from your enemy and made appointment with you at the right side of the mount and sent down upon you manna and quails.﴾ [81] ﴿Eat from the good things with which We have provided you, but do not transgress therein, lest My anger descend upon you. And he on whom My anger descends has certainly fallen.﴾ [Ta-Ha: 80–81].

﴿O Children of Israel, We had certainly delivered you from your enemy﴾, who was Pharaoh and his people. They had subjected you to the worst torment: they slaughtered your sons and spared your women. This was by drowning them while you were watching, so that your eyes were comforted by them. ﴿And made appointment with you at the right side of the mount﴾, meaning: for the secret conversation with Musa and the sending down of the Torah upon him. The Samaritan Jews claim that this mountain is in Nablus, and they call it the Mount of Tur; it is mentioned in geography under the name ʿIbal, and they have an annual festival in which they ascend to it and offer sacrifices there. And Allah knows best.

Al-Zamakhshari said: The appointment was attributed to them only because it concerned them and was connected with them, since it was for their prophet and their leaders. And its benefits returned to them, through which their religion and their law were established, and through what He bestowed upon them of His other blessings and provisions.

"Janiba" (the side) is an adverbial accusative (maf'ul fihi), or an object accusative by extension (ittisa'), or by supposing an omitted noun, meaning: the coming to a side. ﴿And sent down upon you manna and quails﴾. ﴿Eat from the good things with which We have provided you﴾ [Ta-Ha: 81], meaning: from its delicacies, for the manna is like honey, and the quails are birds of good flesh. ﴿But do not transgress therein﴾ [Ta-Ha: 81], meaning: concerning what We have provided you, by exceeding the limits of Allah in it and opposing what he was commanded. ﴿Lest My anger descend upon you, and he on whom My anger descends has certainly fallen﴾ [Ta-Ha: 81], meaning: has perished.

Then He mentioned His blessings upon the Children of Israel and His great favours, and what He enjoined upon them of guarding gratitude for them, and warned them against exposing themselves to His wrath through disbelief in them, by His saying, glorified is He:

(p-4199) The Discussion on the Interpretation of His Words, Exalted is He:

[82] ﴿And indeed, I am Most Forgiving toward one who repents, believes, does righteous deeds, and then remains guided.﴾

﴿And indeed, I am Most Forgiving toward one who repents, believes, does righteous deeds, and then remains guided.﴾ That is: he repents of whatever he was engaged in of disbelief, polytheism, disobedience, or hypocrisy, and does righteous deeds with his limbs, ﴿then remains guided﴾, i.e., he stays upright and firm upon the guidance mentioned, which is repentance, faith, and righteous deeds. A similar statement is His, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, those who say, "Our Lord is Allah," and then remain steadfast﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 13]. In the verse there is encouragement for one who has fallen into the pit of transgression, by explaining the way out of it for him, so that he does not despair.

The commentary on His words, exalted is He:

The discussion on the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[83] ﴿And what has hastened you away from your people, O Moses?﴾

﴿And what has hastened you away from your people, O Moses?﴾ That is: what thing hastened you away from them, as a rebuke (ʿalā sabīl al-inkār). The elders (al-nuqabāʾ) whom he had chosen from his people had gone with him to al-Ṭūr at the appointed time, and then he went ahead of them out of longing for the speech of his Lord and His pleasure.

**The interpretation of His saying, the Exalted:**

[84] ﴿He said, "They are right behind me, and I hastened to You, my Lord, that You may be pleased."﴾

﴿He said, "They are right behind me"﴾: that is, they are coming, descending with the Tur (Mount Sinai). I only outpaced them with what I thought to be good. Therefore he said: ﴿And I hastened to You, my Lord, that You may be pleased﴾, that is, with me, by my hurrying to carry out Your command and my care to fulfil Your covenant. The addition of "my Lord" (rabbi) is for greater humble supplication and entreaty, desiring that the excuse be accepted. This is what Abu al-Su'ud conveyed.

(p-4200) If it is said: the expected answer to Musa's question would have been that he asks for an increase in Your pleasure, or yearning for Your speech. The answer is that this is a failure to grasp the secret of the disapproving question. The reason is that the disapproval is, in essence, directed at the separation and detachment from them. It is thus focused on the restriction (qayd), as is known in similar cases. So the question, in meaning, is about the separation that is implied by (a'jalaka), the verb that is transitive with (min). And the denial concerns the haste because it is a means to that separation. So the answer is: ﴿They are right behind me﴾. His saying ﴿And I hastened﴾ and so on is a completion. It has also been said that the answer is only his saying ﴿And I hastened﴾ and so on, and what precedes it is a preface to it.

Al-Nasir said: God, who knows best, asked him about the cause of the haste only to teach Musa the etiquette of travel. That etiquette is that the leader of a people should lag behind them in walking, so that his view encompasses his group, his authority reaches them, and he watches over them. This meaning is not achieved by going ahead of them. Do you not see how God, Mighty and Majestic, taught this etiquette to Lut, saying: ﴿And follow their rear﴾ [al-Hijr: 65], commanding him to be the last of them. Moreover, Musa, peace be upon him, neglected this matter only out of haste to earn God's pleasure, and hurrying to the appointment. That is the state of one promised something that gladdens him; he wishes that wings of birds were fitted to him. Nothing is more delightful than God's promise to him, (ﷺ)... [sic: peace be upon him]. End quote.

**The interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:**

[85] ﴿He said, "Indeed, We have tried your people after you, and al-Samiri has led them astray."﴾

﴿He said, "Indeed, We have tried your people after you"﴾, meaning: We tested them after your departure for the intimate conversation (munajah) with Us. ﴿And al-Samiri has led them astray﴾, meaning the Jew who whispered to them to worship a calf that they would take as a god, when Musa's absence was prolonged for them and they despaired of his return. "Al-Samiri," in the language of the Arabs, means the Jew. Whoever claimed to know his name or tried to identify him has spoken by conjecture. As for the Samaritan sect today, they are a group of Jews in Nablus, small in number, who differ from the rest of the Jews in most of their customs.

This sentence, by which I mean His, exalted is He, informing Musa of the trial, contains the command to return to his people and to correct what had become corrupt of their condition, as He, exalted is He, said:

The discussion of His saying, may He be exalted:

[86] ﴿So Moses returned to his people, angry and grieved. He said, "O my people, did your Lord not make you a good promise? Did the time seem long to you, or did you desire that wrath from your Lord should descend upon you, so that you broke your appointment with me?"﴾

﴿So Moses returned to his people, angry and grieved﴾: i.e., sorrowful. ﴿He said, "O my people, did your Lord not make you a good promise?"﴾ i.e., by sending down the Torah to me and my returning with it to you. ﴿"Did the time seem long to you?"﴾ i.e., the period until the fulfilment, or my coming. ﴿"Or did you desire that wrath from your Lord should descend upon you, so that you broke your appointment with me?"﴾ i.e., your promise to me to remain steadfast in what I commanded you until I return from the appointed meeting.

The discussion on the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[87] ﴿They said, "We did not break our promise to you by our own will, but we were burdened with loads of the ornaments of the people, so we threw them, and that is how al-Samiri cast."﴾ [88] ﴿Then he brought out for them a calf, a body that lowed, and they said, "This is your god and the god of Musa, but he forgot."﴾ (Ta-Ha: 88).

﴿They said, "We did not break our promise to you by our own will"﴾ It was recited with all three vowel markings (harakat) on the letter mim (in bimalkina, "by our own will").

It has been said that it became alive and lowed as a calf lows. It has also been said that life did not enter it, but he made in it vents and holes, such that the winds would enter them and a sound resembling the lowing of a calf would come out. This was related by al-Razi.

As for His saying, ﴿they said﴾, that is, al-Samiri and those who were led astray by him, ﴿"This is your god and the god of Musa, but he forgot"﴾ (Ta-Ha: 88), that is, he (Musa) forgot it and went off seeking it on the Tur (Mount Sinai). Then God, exalted is He, denounced those who were led astray by this calf and who led others astray, deeming them foolish for what they had undertaken, which no one could mistake for falsehood, in His saying, glorified is He:

(p-4203) On the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:

[91] ﴿They said, "We will not cease to be devoted to it until Moses returns to us."﴾ [92] ﴿He said, "O Harun, what prevented you, when you saw them going astray,"﴾ [Ta-Ha: 92] [93] ﴿"from following me? Have you then disobeyed my command?"﴾ [Ta-Ha: 93].

﴿They said, "We will not cease to be devoted to it until Moses returns to us."﴾ ﴿He said﴾ [Ta-Ha: 92], i.e., Moses: ﴿"O Harun, what prevented you, when you saw them going astray,"﴾ [Ta-Ha: 92] ﴿"from following me?"﴾ [Ta-Ha: 93], i.e., in zeal for God and in the severity of rebuking them for disbelief. And the "la" is not superfluous. Or the meaning is: "What led you to not follow me?", by taking the opposite to mean the opposite, for preventing someone from a thing necessarily entails driving him toward its opposite. Or: "What prevented you from joining me and informing me of their misguidance, so that your departure from them would be a deterrent to them?" ﴿"Have you then disobeyed my command?"﴾ [Ta-Ha: 93], which is what he had commanded him: that he should succeed him among his people and set right what he saw to be corrupt.

﴿He said: "I perceived what they did not perceive"﴾, meaning: I was perceptive of what they were not perceptive of. ﴿So I took a handful from the footprint of the Messenger and threw it﴾, meaning: into the melted ornaments, until it lowed. ﴿Thus did my soul make it seem appealing to me﴾, meaning: it made it good and adorned it for me. ﴿He said: "Go, for in this life it is yours to say, 'No touching.' And you have"﴾ [Ta-Ha 20:97], meaning: for your punishment, ﴿an appointment that you will not be able to break. Look at your god to which you remained devoted: we will surely burn it, then scatter it into the sea in scattering"﴾ [Ta-Ha 20:97], meaning: we will surely blow it away as ash into the sea, such that no trace or remnant of it remains.

**Remarks (tanbihat):**

**First:** Know that Harun (Aaron), peace be upon him, followed in this admonition the most excellent of approaches. He first restrained them from falsehood with his saying: ﴿You are only being tested by it﴾ [Ta-Ha 20:90]. Second, he called them to the knowledge of God, Exalted is He, with his saying: ﴿Indeed, your Lord is the Most Merciful﴾ [Ta-Ha 20:90]. Third, he called them to knowledge of prophethood with the saying of God, Exalted is He: ﴿So follow me﴾ [Ta-Ha 20:90]. Fourth, he called them to the legal laws (shara'i') with his saying: ﴿And obey my command﴾ [Ta-Ha 20:90]. This is the good order, for before everything it is necessary to clear harm from the path, which is the removal of doubts; then the knowledge of God, Exalted is He, for it is the root; then prophethood; then the Law. Thus it is established that this order is in the most excellent manner. This was stated by al-Razi.

God, Exalted is He, has cleared, through these clear verses, Harun, peace be upon him, of what the scribes of the Torah [p-4205] attributed to him, that he was the Samiri who made the calf and commanded its worship, as is found among them. This is among the greatest of fabrications, without doubt.

**Second:** Most exegetes said: the intended meaning of "the Messenger" in the saying of God, Exalted is He, ﴿I took a handful from the footprint of the Messenger﴾ is Jibril (Gabriel), peace be upon him. By "his footprint" they meant the dust he took from the place where his mount's hoof had struck. Then they differed on when the Samiri saw him: it was said he saw him on the day the sea was split, and it was said he saw him at the time of Musa's going to Mount Tur.

They also differed on how the Samiri came to be singled out for seeing Jibril, peace be upon him, and recognizing him among all other people. It was said he recognized him because he had seen him in his childhood, and because he was saved from the killing of Pharaoh's people, and that Jibril was among those who raised him. All of this has no basis in knowledge, and the noble revelation does not indicate it. Therefore Abu Muslim al-Isfahani said: there is no explicit statement in the Qur'an of what the exegetes mentioned. Here there is another view: that the intended meaning of "the Messenger" is Musa, peace be upon him, and by "his footprint" is his way and the mark he commanded. A man may say: "So-and-so follows the footprint of so-and-so and takes hold of his trace," when he complies with his practice. The meaning is that when Musa, peace be upon him, turned to the Samiri with blame and questioned him about the matter that had led him to mislead the people concerning the calf, he said: ﴿I perceived what they did not perceive﴾, meaning: I knew that what you are upon is not true, and I had taken a handful from your footprint, O Messenger, meaning: some of your way and religion. ﴿So I threw it﴾, meaning: I cast it away. At that point Musa, peace be upon him, informed him of the punishment he would have in this world and the Hereafter. He used the form of speaking about an absent person, as a man says to his chief while facing him: "What does the Amir say about such-and-such? What does the Amir command?"

As for his calling Musa, peace be upon him, a messenger despite his denial and disbelief, this is according to the view of those whom God, Exalted is He, quoted as saying: ﴿And they said, "O you to whom the Reminder has been sent, indeed you are a madman"﴾ [al-Hijr 15:6], even though they did not believe in the sending down. End of quotation.

[p-4206] al-Razi said: What Abu Muslim mentioned is closer to verification than what the exegetes mentioned, for several reasons:

First: Jibril, peace be upon him, is not known by the name "the Messenger," and no mention of him has preceded, so that the definite article would be made to refer to him. Using the word "the Messenger" to mean Jibril, peace be upon him, is like imposing the knowledge of the unseen.

Second: it requires an ellipsis (idmar), namely: "a handful from the trace of the hoof of the Messenger's horse," and ellipsis contradicts the basic principle.

Third: it requires strained explanation of how the Samiri came to be singled out from among all people for seeing Jibril, peace be upon him, and recognizing him. Then how did he know that the dust of his horse's hoof had this effect? As for what they mentioned, that Jibril, peace be upon him, was the one who raised him, it is far-fetched. For if the Samiri recognized Jibril while in full possession of his reason, he would certainly have known that Musa, peace be upon him, was a truthful prophet; how then would he try to mislead? And if what he recognized was in the state of having reached puberty, what benefit is there in Jibril having been his tutor during childhood in gaining that knowledge? End of quotation.

**Third remark:** Regarding His saying: ﴿No touching﴾ [Ta-Ha 20:97], there are several views:

First: "I do not touch, and I am not touched."

Second: the intended meaning is a prohibition on mixing with anyone, or anyone mixing with him, as a punishment for him.

Third: what Abu Muslim mentioned, that it is possible to interpret it as: "I do not want to touch women." Then God's punishment of him would be the cutting off of his offspring, so that he would have no child to console him. God, Exalted is He, would thus strip him of the two adornments of this world that He mentioned in His saying: ﴿Wealth and children are the adornment of the life of this world﴾ [al-Kahf 18:46]. That is, because "touching" is used as a euphemism for intercourse, as in the verse: ﴿Before you touch them﴾ [al-Ahzab 33:49]. And God knows best.

[p-4207] When Musa, peace be upon him, had finished refuting what the Samiri had called to, he returned to explaining the true religion, and said:
